slides.title: Modifiers, Access Control & Error Handling
slides.subtitle: Lecture #5 — Writing Secure, Clean, Professional Solidity
slides.tagline: Every professional Solidity contract — ERC20, NFT, DeFi, DAO — uses modifiers. This lecture shows you how.

slides.title: Why Modifiers Matter — The Real-World Case
slides.definition: Every professional Solidity contract uses modifiers. Whether you are building an ERC-20 token, an NFT collection, a DeFi staking protocol, or a DAO — the same access control pattern appears everywhere. Today you will learn to write it the professional way.
keyPoints: ERC-20 tokens: only the contract owner can mint new tokens or pause transfers — onlyOwner modifier on mint() and pause()
NFT projects: only the owner can set the base URI, reveal the collection, or withdraw ETH — onlyOwner on every admin function
DeFi staking: only the protocol admin can change reward rates, set fee receivers, or upgrade logic — protected by access control modifiers
DAO contracts: only approved governance proposals can execute on-chain actions — checked via modifier before any state change
OpenZeppelin (the most trusted Solidity library) ships Ownable.sol — a standard contract that provides the onlyOwner modifier — used in millions of deployed contracts
Goal of today: understand why modifiers exist, write them from scratch, and use all three Solidity error tools: require(), revert(), assert()

slides.title: Real-Life Analogy — The Bank Manager
slides.subtitle: Introduction — 10 min
slides.analogy: Imagine a bank. Any customer (Ali, Ahmed, Sara, John) can walk in, check balances, and make deposits. BUT only the Bank Manager can approve loans, change bank settings, or access the reserve account vault. Customers cannot do these things — not because they are bad people, but because those actions require special authority.
leftItems: Check own balance
Deposit money
Withdraw own funds
View public info
rightItems: Approve loans
Change bank settings
Transfer from reserve
Hire / fire employees
slides.bottomNote: In Solidity: public functions = customer counter. onlyOwner functions = manager's office. The modifier is the door with a keycard.

slides.title: The Problem — Code Duplication
slides.subtitle: Part 1 — Why modifiers exist: writing require() 50 times is a serious problem

codeBlocks.label: Bad Pattern — Same Code Written 3+ Times

keyPoints: require(msg.sender == owner, 'Not Owner') appears 3 times here — in a real contract it appears 10, 20, even 50 times
Code Duplication: writing identical code in multiple places — one of the most serious problems in software engineering
Problem 1 — Maintenance: if you need to change the error message from 'Not Owner' to 'Access Denied', you must change it in every function
Problem 2 — Bugs: copy-paste errors; you might forget to add require() to one function, leaving a security hole
Problem 3 — Readability: 50 functions, each starting with require() — the code becomes long and hard to read
Problem 4 — Unprofessional: senior auditors and developers immediately notice code duplication as a red flag
Solution: write the check ONCE in a modifier — then attach that modifier to every function that needs it
practicalSteps: Count how many times require(msg.sender == owner) appears in this contract
Imagine this pattern across 20 functions — how many lines of repeated code?
Ask: what if we need to add a second condition to the owner check? How many places to update?

slides.title: Code Duplication vs Modifiers — Side by Side
slides.subtitle: Part 1 — The Problem Visualised
slides.badNote: Same code written 5 times. Change one thing → update 5 places. Miss one → security hole.
slides.goodNote: Logic written ONCE. Applied everywhere. Change one place → all functions updated automatically.

slides.title: What is a Modifier?
slides.definition: A modifier is a reusable piece of code that executes BEFORE (or after) a function body. It is attached to functions like a keyword. When the function is called, the modifier runs first — checks a condition — and only if the check passes, the actual function body executes.
keyPoints: Think of a modifier as a 'gate' or 'bouncer' placed in front of a function — it decides whether the function is allowed to run
Modifiers are defined once at the contract level (like functions) and then applied to as many functions as needed
The special placeholder _; (underscore semicolon) marks where the actual function body will execute
Without _; in a modifier — the function body NEVER runs; the underscore is mandatory
Modifiers can take parameters: modifier minAmount(uint _min) { require(msg.value >= _min); _; }
Multiple modifiers on one function: function action() public onlyOwner notPaused { } — both run in left-to-right order
Modifiers can also run code AFTER the function: place code after _; for post-execution checks

slides.title: How a Modifier Works — Execution Flow
slides.subtitle: Part 2 — Modifier Syntax
leftItems: User calls function
Modifier runs first
require() checks condition
_; — function body runs
Return value to caller
slides.leftDesc: The modifier wraps the function — pre-condition check → function → optional post check
rightItems: Condition TRUE → _; → function executes
Condition FALSE → REVERT → function blocked
No state changes saved on revert
Error message returned to caller
Gas used up to revert is consumed
slides.rightDesc: The modifier is the security checkpoint before any privileged function can execute
slides.outcomeDesc: The underscore _; is where the actual function body is injected — without it the function never runs

slides.title: Modifier Syntax — Every Word Explained
slides.subtitle: Part 2 — Write your first modifier from scratch

codeBlocks.label: Modifier Anatomy — Fully Labelled

keyPoints: modifier — keyword telling Solidity 'I am defining a reusable check, not a function'
onlyOwner — the modifier's NAME; written exactly like this on every function that needs owner-only access
() — parentheses; modifiers can accept parameters like functions; empty () for no parameters
require(msg.sender == owner, 'Not Owner') — the actual check; runs BEFORE the function body
_; — THE MOST IMPORTANT PART: this is where the function body executes; without _; the function never runs
public onlyOwner on withdraw() — visibility first, then modifier; both are listed in the function signature
Code flow: withdraw() called → onlyOwner modifier runs → require check → if passes: _; runs withdraw body → done
practicalSteps: Write modifier onlyOwner with just _; — observe the function runs for EVERYONE
Add require(msg.sender == owner) before _; — now only owner can run the function
Remove _; — deploy and call the function — notice it does NOTHING (body never executes)
This proves _; is what connects the modifier to the function body

slides.title: Practical 1 — OwnerExample Contract
slides.subtitle: First complete contract using onlyOwner modifier — deploy and test in Remix

codeBlocks.label: OwnerExample.sol

keyPoints: address public owner — state variable storing the owner's wallet address; public = readable by anyone
constructor() { owner = msg.sender; } — runs once at deployment; msg.sender at that moment = deployer wallet
modifier onlyOwner() — defined once between the constructor and functions; reusable on any function
getOwner() — no modifier; anyone can call this; it is a public view function returning the owner address
secretMessage() public onlyOwner pure — notice the modifier is placed between public and pure; the modifier is the security layer
Students MUST test: call secretMessage() as owner → succeeds. Switch account → call again → REVERTS: 'Not Owner'
The error message 'Not Owner' is returned in the Remix console — show students how to read it
practicalSteps: Deploy with Wallet A (Account 1 in Remix)
Call getOwner() → returns Wallet A's address
Call secretMessage() as Wallet A → 'Only Owner Can Read This'
Switch to Account 2 in Remix → call secretMessage() → REVERT: 'Not Owner'
Students see that ONE modifier protects the function — no require() written inside the function

slides.title: Practical 2 — Counter with onlyOwner
slides.subtitle: Only the contract owner can increment — demonstrates real access control

codeBlocks.label: Counter.sol — Access Controlled

keyPoints: onlyOwner modifier defined ONCE — applied to both increment() and reset() — zero code duplication
If we had 10 admin functions, the modifier is still defined once — that is the entire point
count++ and count = 0 are state changes — they cost gas and create transactions — only owner pays and decides
getCount() has no modifier — anyone can READ the count for free; reading is always open
What happens with Account 2: increment() → REVERT 'Not Owner' | getCount() → works fine (no modifier)
This pattern is the EXACT same pattern used in Compound Finance, Aave, and Uniswap admin functions
Modifier reuse benefit: to change the access rule for ALL admin functions — edit ONE modifier, not every function
practicalSteps: Deploy with Account 1 (owner)
Call increment() as Account 1 → count = 1 → transaction succeeds
Call increment() as Account 2 → REVERT: 'Not Owner' → count stays at 1
Call getCount() as Account 2 → works, returns 1 (public view, no modifier)
Call reset() as Account 1 → count = 0
Point out: two functions protected by one modifier definition — professional pattern

slides.title: Part 3 — Error Handling: Three Tools in Solidity
leftItems: Purpose: validate external conditions — user input, balances, permissions, state
Syntax: require(condition, 'error message');
If condition is FALSE → REVERT with message → gas up to this point consumed
If condition is TRUE → execution continues normally
Most common error tool — used in almost every function
Examples: require(amount > 0), require(msg.sender == owner), require(balance >= amount)
Gas refund: unused gas is refunded to the caller after a require() revert
rightItems: require() → use for: checking user-provided values, access control, balance checks, state preconditions — anything that depends on external input
revert() → use for: complex conditions that need if-else logic; when require() syntax is too rigid; custom error types in Solidity 0.8.4+
assert() → use for: internal invariants that should mathematically NEVER be false; detecting bugs in your own logic; NOT for user input
Rule of thumb: if a user could possibly cause the condition to be false → use require(). If only a bug in YOUR code could cause it → use assert()
Gas behaviour: require() and revert() refund unused gas; assert() in older Solidity consumed ALL gas (Panic in 0.8.x is more lenient)
Frequency: require() = very common | revert() = less common | assert() = rare; most contracts have zero assert() calls

slides.title: revert() — Manual Revert with Custom Logic
slides.subtitle: Part 3 — Use revert() when require() is too rigid for complex conditions

codeBlocks.label: revert() vs require() — Same Result, Different Style

keyPoints: revert('message') — immediately stops execution and reverts all state changes; identical end result to require(false, 'message')
When to prefer revert(): when you have multiple conditions checked in sequence with different logic paths
revert() inside an if block — more readable for complex multi-branch logic than chaining require() statements
Custom errors (Solidity 0.8.4+): error NotOwner(address caller); then revert NotOwner(msg.sender); — saves ~50% gas vs string message
Both require() and revert() refund all unused gas after the revert point
The Remix console shows the exact revert reason string — students should learn to read it to debug their contracts
In practice: use require() for simple single-condition checks; use revert() when you need if-else branching
practicalSteps: Deploy contract with both withdrawA and withdrawB
Call both as owner → both succeed identically
Call both as non-owner → both REVERT with 'Not Owner'
Observe: the result is identical — only the coding style differs
Try complexCheck(0) → REVERT: 'Zero amount' | complexCheck(2000) → REVERT: 'Amount too high'

slides.title: assert() — Internal Bug Detection
slides.subtitle: Part 3 — assert() is for YOUR code logic, never for user input validation

codeBlocks.label: All Three Error Tools — Complete Demo

keyPoints: testRequire(0) → REVERT: 'Amount must be > 0' — correct use: checking external input from the user
testRequire(10) → passes — amount > 0 is satisfied, execution continues
testRevert() as non-owner → REVERT: 'Not Owner — use revert style' — same as require but if-else style
testAssert() → passes (5 + 3 == 8 is always true) — assert verifies OUR own math is correct
assert() would only fail if there is a BUG in the contract code itself — not because a user did something wrong
Solidity 0.8.x: failed assert() throws a Panic(uint256) error — different from require/revert Error(string)
Never use assert() to check user input or msg.sender — those are user-facing conditions, use require()
practicalSteps: Deploy ErrorExample
testRequire(0) → REVERT: 'Amount must be > 0'
testRequire(5) → succeeds (no return value, just passes)
testRevert() as owner → passes | as non-owner → REVERT
testAssert() → always passes (5+3=8 always) — change 8 to 9 in code → redeploy → PANIC

slides.title: Putting It All Together — Professional Bank Contract
slides.subtitle: Final practical: onlyOwner modifier + all three error tools in one real contract

codeBlocks.label: ProfessionalBank.sol

keyPoints: TWO modifiers: onlyOwner (access control) and notPaused (state check) — both defined once, reused everywhere
deposit() public payable notPaused — open to everyone but blocked when paused; require(msg.value > 0) = input validation
pause() public onlyOwner — only owner can pause; no logic inside the function itself — the modifier does all checking
unpause() public onlyOwner — same modifier, different function — one modifier definition protects both
getVaultBalance() public view onlyOwner — a view function CAN have a modifier; modifier runs before the return
Multiple modifiers order: function action() public onlyOwner notPaused — onlyOwner runs first, then notPaused, then body
This pattern is identical to OpenZeppelin's Pausable.sol + Ownable.sol — the industry standard access control library
practicalSteps: Deploy — owner = Account 1
Deposit 1 ETH as Account 2 → succeeds
Owner calls pause() → paused = true
Try deposit() again → REVERT: 'Contract is paused'
Owner calls unpause() → deposit works again
Account 2 tries getVaultBalance() → REVERT: 'Not Owner'
Owner calls getVaultBalance() → shows total ETH

slides.title: Real-World Usage — Modifiers in Production Contracts
slides.leftTitle: Where You See This in the Wild
leftItems: OpenZeppelin Ownable.sol — the standard: modifier onlyOwner() { require(owner() == _msgSender(), 'Ownable: caller is not the owner'); _; } — used in every serious project
ERC-20 tokens: function mint(address to, uint amount) public onlyOwner — new tokens can only be created by the contract deployer
NFT contracts: function setBaseURI(string memory uri) external onlyOwner — metadata URL controlled by owner only
Uniswap V2: modifier ensure(uint deadline) { require(deadline >= block.timestamp, 'EXPIRED'); _; } — a modifier with a PARAMETER checking transaction deadline
Aave protocol: modifier onlyPoolAdmin() — checks caller is in the admin role mapping; same concept, more complex implementation
Chainlink oracles: modifier onlyOwner and modifier validChainlinkRequest — multiple modifiers stacked on one function
rightItems: Task 1: Voting Contract — add modifier onlyAdmin() that restricts addCandidate() to admin only; anyone can call vote(candidateId); use mapping(address => bool) hasVoted with require(!hasVoted[msg.sender]) in the vote function

Task 2: Token Contract — state variables: string name, string symbol, uint totalSupply, mapping(address=>uint) balances; modifier onlyOwner on mint(); function transfer(address to, uint amount) uses require(balances[msg.sender] >= amount)

Task 3: Timed Auction — modifier onlyWhileOpen() that checks block.timestamp < auctionEndTime; bid() is payable with onlyWhileOpen; require(msg.value > highestBid); owner can call endAuction() to close
Challenge: Add a second modifier validAddress(address _addr) that does require(_addr != address(0), 'Zero address') — apply it to any function that takes an address parameter
Explore: Read OpenZeppelin Ownable.sol on GitHub — find onlyOwner modifier definition and compare with what we wrote today

slides.title: Lecture #5 Summary — Key Takeaways
points: Code duplication — writing require() in 20 functions — is a serious bug risk, maintenance nightmare, and mark of unprofessional code
A modifier is a reusable code block that runs BEFORE a function; defined once with modifier onlyOwner() { require(...); _; }
The _; (underscore semicolon) is mandatory — it marks where the actual function body executes; without it the function never runs
owner = msg.sender in the constructor captures the deployer address; the onlyOwner modifier then restricts privileged functions to only that address
require(condition, 'message') — the primary guard for user-facing checks: input validation, access control, balance checks — most common error tool
revert('message') — identical result to require(false) but more flexible for complex if-else branches and custom error types
assert(condition) — for internal code invariants only; proves YOUR OWN logic is correct; never use for user input; Panic error on failure
Multiple modifiers stack on one function: function action() public onlyOwner notPaused — each runs in order before the function body
slides.closing: One modifier written once protects dozens of functions. This is how professional, secure, auditable Solidity is written.
